judge_assessment.explanation: The judge's values are all correct and I re-derived each: y = 2x^4 - 3x^2 + C with y(1) = 4 giving C = 5 and y(2) = 25; dy/dx = 2xy with y(0) = 3 giving y = 3e^(x^2) and y(1) = 3e = 8.15; dy/dx = 5y with y(0) = 6 giving y = 6e^(5x) and y(1) = 6e^5 = 890.48; y dy = x dx giving y^2 = x^2 + 16 and y(3) = 5; -1/y = x - 1/2 giving y = 1/(0.5 - x) and y(0.25) = 4; and y = 3 ln(x^2 + 1) + 2 giving y(2) = 3 ln 5 + 2 = 6.83. The refutation in problem 8 is correct as the judge describes. Two findings the 32/32 does not record. First, the sheet's own directions say "Where a student's work is shown, (i) name the first wrong line, (ii) say what rule it breaks, (iii) solve correctly", so problems 3, 4, 5 and 6 each print two written slots ahead of the number, and problems 1, 2, 6 and 7 print further written demands ("say in one phrase what that constant represents on a slope field"; "State the step at which the initial condition may first be used"; "say what the corrected solution does as x approaches 0.5, and why that behaviour is invisible in Sam's version"; "explain why applying the initial condition before integrating would be meaningless"). Every one of them sits inside an `approx`, `eval` or `integrate` entry; only problem 8 is typed manual. Second, and more concretely wrong on the page: Quick Answers item 1 prints "2x^4 - 3x^2" for a problem whose printed instruction is "Find the general solution ... Include the constant of integration". The answer key's own boxed answer is y = 2x^4 - 3x^2 + C. A general solution without its constant is not a different form of the right answer, it is an incomplete one, printed in the column a teacher grades from -- and it is the exact error the rest of the sheet is built to diagnose.

strengths_to_preserve: Six declared traps whose wrong-method expressions reproduce, number for number, the values printed in the fictional students' work: 20 (dropping C before evaluating), 4 (integrating with y treated as a constant), 153.41 (exp(5) + 5), 7 (3 + 4 from rooting termwise), 1.33 (1/(0.25 + 0.5) with the sign lost) and 4.83 (the antiderivative without C).

Problem 7 asks the student to predict "what answer a student who forgets the constant of integration entirely would report" -- and that value, 4.83, is exactly the trap the verify data already derives for that problem. Asking the student to compute the misconception rather than only avoid it is the strongest item on the sheet.

The three named failure modes are stated as a checklist in the directions (integrating before separating; losing or misplacing C; applying the initial condition at the wrong step) and each of problems 3-6 instantiates exactly one of them, so the sheet's diagnosis vocabulary is fixed before the first problem.

Problem 5's error -- "take the square root of both sides" giving y = x + C -- is the sum-of-squares misconception, and the key repairs it by carrying y^2 = x^2 + 16 through to y(3) = 5 rather than only naming the rule.

root_causes.description: An error-analysis item can print a named-error slot and a rule-citation slot alongside its repaired value while the verify data records only the value, so the sheet's diagnostic content sits entirely outside the verification contract.
evidence: worksheet directions: "(i) name the first wrong line, (ii) say what rule it breaks, (iii) solve correctly"
verify.json types problems 1-7 as integrate/eval/approx; only problem 8 is manual

problem 1 also asks what C represents on a slope field, problem 2 for the step at which the initial condition may first be used, problem 6 for the behaviour as x -> 0.5, and problem 7 for why applying the condition before integrating would be meaningless -- none has an entry

root_causes.description: For an `integrate` entry the expected value is by contract an antiderivative without its constant, and the Quick Answers bank prints that value verbatim, so a general-solution problem shows an incomplete answer in the grading column.
evidence: worksheet problem 1: "Find the general solution ... Include the constant of integration"
the key's Quick Answers prints "1. 2x^4 - 3x^2" while the worked solution boxes y = 2x^4 - 3x^2 + C

improvements.title: Four find-and-fix items plus four further written demands carry no manual entry
improvements.proposed_change: Add a build gate tests/check_open_response_flags.py, wired into scripts/build.sh next to check_layout.py, that reads the ws_ .tex and the verify JSON together. For each problem body it matches explanation cues (explain / justify / name the error / name the first wrong line / say in one sentence / say what / describe / sketch / state what it tells you / why) and fails the build when that problem id carries no entry of type `manual`. Tighten SKILL.md's rule from "Use manual for ... any explanation/reasoning answer" to the explicit statement that a problem mixing a computed answer with a written justification needs BOTH entries under the same id -- the multi-entry-per-id shape verify.py already supports and that curr-445 already uses correctly.
improvements.regression_test: tests/test_open_response_flags.py::test_explanation_without_manual_entry_fails -- a fixture worksheet whose problem 2 reads "Solve ... then explain in one sentence why the negative candidate is extraneous" with verify.json holding only {"id": 2, "type": "solve", ...} must exit non-zero and name problem 2; the same fixture with an added {"id": 2, "type": "manual"} entry must exit 0. Today no such gate exists, so the first fixture builds green.
improvements.expected_impact: Every written justification the sheet demands becomes visible as a manual-review item (exit 2) instead of being absorbed into a "fully machine-verified" claim, which is what the task prompt asks for.
improvements.risk: Cue matching over prose will over-fire on stems that merely say "show your work"; keep the cue list narrow, exempt ids already typed `manual`, and fixture-lock both the firing and the non-firing case.

improvements.title: Quick Answers drops the +C on the problem that demands the constant of integration
improvements.proposed_change: In scripts/render_quick_answers.py, stop round-tripping a string `expected` through sympify -> sympy.latex, which re-normalises the author's answer into SymPy's canonical form and spelling. Three changes: (1) accept an optional per-entry `expected_tex` in the verify JSON and prefer it verbatim when present; (2) when falling back to sympify, parse with evaluate=False and print with order='none' so a factored argument stays factored; (3) apply a spelling map before printing (atan/asin/acos -> \arctan/\arcsin/\arccos, log(a)/log(b) -> \log_b a, and ln for the natural log) and append "+ C" for entries of type `integrate`, whose expected is by contract an antiderivative without its constant.
improvements.regression_test: tests/test_render_quick_answers.py::test_bank_preserves_authored_form -- a verify fixture with entries expected "4*sin(3*(x - pi/6))", "atan(x) + x/(1 + x**2)" and an `integrate` entry expected "2*x**4-3*x**2" must render a factored sine (not -4\cos(3x)), \arctan (not \operatorname{atan}) and a trailing "+ C". Today all three assertions fail: sympy.latex(sympify("4*sin(3*(x - pi/6))")) returns "- 4 \cos{\left(3 x \right)}" and sympy.latex(sympify("atan(x)")) returns "\operatorname{atan}{\left(x \right)}".
improvements.expected_impact: The answer key's at-a-glance grading column stops disagreeing with the form, notation and completeness the worksheet asked for, on the one page a teacher grades from.
improvements.risk: Unevaluated printing can produce uglier output for entries that genuinely wanted simplification, and the spelling map must not corrupt an expected value that legitimately contains log. Both are contained by keeping the current renderer as the fallback and fixture-locking the bank text.

case_summary: An outstanding error-analysis packet on separable equations: three named failure modes fixed in the directions, four find-and-fix items each instantiating one of them, six machine-derived traps that reproduce the printed wrong numbers exactly, and one item that asks the student to compute the misconception itself. All the mathematics is correct. Two defects the judge did not record: the diagnosis slots the directions demand on every shown-work item -- naming the first wrong line and the rule it breaks -- sit inside machine-verified entries with only the synthesis typed manual; and the Quick Answers bank prints the general solution without its +C, which is both a mismatch with the printed instruction and, on this sheet in particular, the very error being taught.
